utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel, thank you very much. Before I beginning my opening statements, I would like to inform the members of the public that I will going -- I will be making exceptional requests to the Trial Chamber to go into closed session because I need to refer to protected documents. I will do so infrequently, sometimes briefly, but I wanted to inform the public of that situation. If I may begin, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: War, which had lain dormant on this continent for half a century, was reawakened in the 1990s, and its scourge was visited on the peoples of Bosnia and Croatia. New benchmarks of human depravity were added to history's long list of horrors: Srebrenica, the siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing. The ambitions and ethnocentric fantasies of politicians fuelled the war, and this war laid waste to parts of Bosnia and Croatia. During this period, Slobodan Milosevic sought to deceive his international interlocutors, the international community, and the public with false claims that the governments of which he was a member and the instruments of those governments, including the army, were not interfering in the affairs of Bosnia and not providing material support and aid to the Bosnian Serb army and to the Bosnian Croat army. His deceits and the deceits of his associates fooled no one. This case, Your Honour, will pierce the veil of elaborate deceptions and will expose the roles of Momcilo Perisic, one of Milosevic's principal collaborators, and will expose his unstinting support for Milosevic's policies to establish a single state of the Serbian people. Now, throughout my remarks, Your Honour, I'm going to be using a number of acronyms. I'm going to be referring to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as the FRY; the Socialist Federative Republic as the SFRY; the Yugoslav People's Army as the JNA; and the Yugoslav Army as the VJ. The accused, Your Honour, was the highest ranking member of the Yugoslav Army chief -- of the army. He was the VJ Chief of the General Staff. He was appointed to that position on the 26th of August, 1993, and he remained in that position until the 24th of November, 1998. In his capacity as Chief of the General Staff, he had the overall authority and responsibility for the functioning of the army. General Perisic was a career military officer, having graduated from the military academy in 1966. He held a number of important positions in both the JNA and the VJ throughout his career, including serving as the commander of the JNA Artillery School Centre in Zadar. Now, that position should be borne in mind, Your Honours, when considering the charges in this indictment, allegations that relate to the 44-month siege and the artillery bombardment of the densely populated city of Sarajevo. In November of 1998, following a disagreement that he had with Slobodan Milosevic over the use of the army in the Kosovo crisis, he was removed from his position as the head of the VJ. Under Yugoslav law, the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in accordance with decisions of the Supreme Defence Council, or SDC, commanded the army in times of war and peace. The SDC was the decision-making body. It was composed of three members - the President of the FRY, Zoran Lilic; the President of the Republic of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic; and the President of the Republic of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic. The SDC debated important and critical issues and formulated state policy. Although not a member of the SDC, Momcilo Perisic attended every session during his tenure as Chief of the VJ General Staff. He participated fully in debates relating to military matters, and he advised members of the SDC on the security situation that affected his government and his nation. He did so because he had the paramount responsibility for both defence and security. He was well informed. He had access to international media. He had access to his colleagues in the adjacent countries of Croatia and Bosnia. In order to implement the policies of the SDC and the President of the FRY, General Perisic issued orders and commands, and we intend to present to Your Honours in our case in chief documents of commands and other sorts of documents that will sustain and will demonstrate his position as Chief of the General Staff. Now, as Chief of the General Staff, General Perisic commanded the army. He did so by issuing orders to his subordinates and to subordinate units. He determined the organisation and establishment of units in the army, and this is particularly important because I will be discussing later in my opening remarks two formations - the 30th and the 40th Personnel Centres - and you'll hear a considerable amount about them during my remarks. General Perisic appointed officers up to the rank of colonel; he retained in the army service officers up to the rank of colonel; he could transfer them; he would issue decisions about their service; he could decide on their termination up to and including the rank of colonel; and he appointed judges and presidents and military disciplinary prosecutors in the military disciplinary court. Outside of the formal sessions of the SDC, General Perisic was a close and frequent collaborator with Slobodan Milosevic, Zoran Lilic, Momir Bulatovic, and his friend General Ratko Mladic. The accused is charged with 13 counts in the present indictment. Those counts relate to events that occurred in Sarajevo, in Srebrenica, and in Zagreb. The Prosecution alleges that he is responsible under both Articles 7.1 and 7.3 for the crimes associated with Sarajevo and Srebrenica, and he is responsible under Article 7.3 for the crimes associated with Zagreb. Now, we focus on the Sarajevo crimes, counts 1 to 4 of the indictment. General Perisic is charged with two counts of murder - one is a crime against humanity, and one is a violation of the laws or customs of war; one count of inhumane acts - injuring and wounding civilians as a crime against humanity; and one count of attacks on civilians, a crime against humanity. All four counts relate to the protracted campaign of shelling and sniping in Sarajevo that resulted in the deaths and killings of thousands of civilians. We allege in the indictment, Your Honours, that these crimes were planned, instigated, ordered, committed and aided by General Perisic's subordinates in the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army, including General Ratko Mladic, including General Stanislav Galic and General Dragomir Milosevic, both of whom were commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, both of -- the latter two have been convicted by this Tribunal. The indictment alleges that General Perisic aided and abetted the commission of these crimes with the knowledge that the assistance he provided would contribute substantially in the commission of those crimes. Schedules A and B of the indictment set forth specific incidents of shelling and sniping, all of which have been litigated in the trials of Generals Galic and Milosevic. In respect of the crimes in Srebrenica, General Perisic is charged with five counts. Those five counts include two counts of murder as a crime against humanity and a violation of the laws and customs of war; one count of inhumane acts, inflicting serious injuries and wounding and forcible transfers as a crime against humanity; one count of persecutions as a crime against humanity; and one count of extermination as a crime against humanity. These five counts relate to events that occurred in July of 1995 in the UN protected area of Srebrenica and its environs, where the VRS, members of the VRS massacred between 7 and 8.000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys and forcibly transferred approximately 25.000 Bosnian Muslims from the enclave. The Prosecution in the indictment alleges that the crimes were planned, instigated, ordered, and aided by General Perisic's associates, subordinates, in the VRS, including General Mladic, whom I've mentioned, General Radislav Krstic, Dragan Obrenovic, Dragan Jokic, Colonel Blagojevic, all of whom have been convicted in this Tribunal for crimes committed in Sarajevo. His other subordinates who've been identified in the indictment include Vinko Pandurevic, Ljubisa Beara, Vujadin Popovic, all of whom are currently on trial for those very same crimes in this institution. Finally, Your Honour, General Perisic is accused of four counts in respect of the events in Zagreb: Two counts of murder, a crime against humanity and a violation of the laws or customs of war; one count of inhumane acts, injuring and wounding civilians as a crime against humanity; and one count of attacks on civilians as a crime against humanity. The charges relate to the missile attacks that took place on the city centre of Zagreb that occurred on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995. The missile attacks were ordered by the President of the Republic of Srpska Krajina Milan Martic and executed by General Perisic's subordinates who served in the Bosnian Croat army. Your Honours, the criminal acts that have been identified in the indictment have been the subject of previous trials in this institution. In fact, many of the facts and events have been judicially established, obviating the need for us to call as witnesses once again people who suffered from those crimes. In pre-trial motions we filed a number of requests asking that the written testimonies and the written statements of witnesses who had testified in previous trials be admitted before Your Honours. The Trial Chamber granted many of those motions, and to the extent that victims are required to testify before Your Honours, we have summoned them to testify and present their evidence to Your Honours in person. In fact, Your Honours, you will hear from some of them very early, at the start of this trial. Our intention, Your Honours, not to call a large number of victims to testify in our case in chief is not out of disrespect or indifference to the victims' sufferings. Their eloquent voices have been repeatedly heard in this institution. Their recorded testimonies and past statements will be introduced to Your Honours for your consideration, and we are indebted to the victims and to the witnesses for the remarkable dignity and courage they displayed when publicly bearing witness to the crimes, the unspeakable crimes, that were inflicted upon them when confronting their tormenters in the courtroom and when recounting the long-lasting effects that those crimes had on their lives. We intend to rely, therefore, in large part on the substantial public record created by their testimonies, their past testimonies, to establish the facts relating to the events underlying the charges. Instead, Your Honours, our evidence will focus on the role of General Perisic in aiding and abetting the commission of crimes alleged in the indictment and on his failure to prevent his subordinates from committing the crimes alleged in the indictment and his failure to punish them for having committed them. In assessing the role of General Perisic, it's necessary to be cognizant of political and military developments that led to the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia and to understand the common objectives of the political and military leaders of Slobodan Milosevic's Serbia and Yugoslavia and their Serb counterparts in Bosnia and in Croatia. I will endeavour to provide Your Honours with a very brief framework. It's not intended to be comprehensive. You will be receiving evidence of expert witnesses. You will be receiving reports of expert witnesses that will touch upon those events in greater depth. In the limited amount of time that's available to me, however, I would like to highlight some of the points that I think will enable you to put the case we're presenting against General Perisic into context. Prior to the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it consisted of six republics and two autonomous regions. In the aftermath of the death of President Tito, latent nationalistic impulses surfaced, and the existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a federal state was questioned. Certain factions favoured independence or a reform of the federal state. Opposing views favoured the preservation of Yugoslavia. The persons who favoured the preservation of Yugoslavia were principally the Serbs of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, led by Slobodan Milosevic; the Bosnian Serbs, led by Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Biljana Plavsic; and the Croatian Serbs, led by Milan Babic, Goran Hadzic, and Milan Martic. The antagonists were unable to resolve their differences peacefully and instead settled them by force of arms. A 10-day war in Slovenia led to the withdrawal of the JNA from that republic, but the armed conflict spread to Croatia where the Croatian Serbs seized and occupied parts of Croatia with the assistance of the JNA and proclaimed the Croatian Serb entity, the Republika Srpska Krajina, or RSK as I'll refer to it. Before that date, in April and May of 1991, the Serb-held territories in Croatia proclaimed themselves a part of Serbia and Yugoslavia. In Bosnia, the developments were different. In Bosnia, in anticipation of multi-party elections that were to occur in November and December of 1990, political parties formed, and the three main political parties were formed principally along ethnic lines. The three parties were the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS, which was led by Radovan Karadzic; the Party of Democratic Action, or the SDA, which was led by Alija Izetbegovic and which was the party of the Bosniaks; and the Croatian Democratic Union, or HDZ, which was the main political party of the Bosnian Croats, which was led by Stjepan Kljujic. The SDS opposed an independent Bosnia, opposed being separated from other Serbs in Yugoslavia, and were prepared to use force if necessary to prevent that from happening. By October of 1991, the issue of prospective Bosnian independence came to a head at a joint session of the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina where a memorandum on independence was to be considered. The Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims favoured the adoption of that memorandum. Radovan Karadzic at that session warned the Muslims that if they pursued independence, they would disappear. After a considerable debate on the issue, the SDS deputies walked out of the assembly, and the deputies who remained - the SDA deputies, the HDZ deputies, and others - voted in favour of the memorandum for independence. Almost immediately after the walkout, the Bosnian Serbs set up parallel bodies of authority, including a Bosnian Serb assembly. They set it up in the same month, October 1991. On the 24th of October, 1991, Karadzic explained to Slobodan Milosevic the following, and I quote: "We are moving on. We will establish full authority over the Serbian territories in Bosnia and none of his lawyers," referring to the lawyers of Alija Izetbegovic, "will be able to show their nose there. He will not be able to exercise power. He will not have control over 65 per cent of his territory. That is our goal." At the same time, the Bosnian Serbs prepared to seize power in large areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina that they considered vital to their interest. As the evidence will show, Your Honours, they did so with the assistance of the JNA. Now, as it became apparent that the federal Yugoslav state would not remain intact and that the republics of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia would not remain in it, the authorities in Belgrade did not remain indifferent. The Belgrade leaders favoured the creation of a state encompassing as many of the Serb inhabitants of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and as much land that they inhabited as possible. The goal of the Serb leaders in the SFRY was the formation of a common Serb state or a union of states. One of the most powerful institutions in the SFRY was the Yugoslav People's Army, or JNA, of which the accused was a high-ranking officer member. According to article 240 of the SFRY constitution, the JNA was the common armed force of all nations and nationalities of the country, meaning he was the common army of the Serbs, the Croats, the Muslims. By December of 1991, with the conflict in Croatia raging and with ethnic relations in Bosnia deteriorating and considerably polarised, the JNA's commitment to ethnic impartiality or neutrality vanished, and the army metamorphosed into the hammer by which Serb interests were to be protected and advanced. Two documents illustrate, Your Honour, the JNA's historic and important shift favouring the Serbs. The first document, if we could have that on the screen, please, the first document was issued -- it should appear on the screen. Yes, it does. The first document, Your Honour, was issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence for the SFRY. It is a -- classified as a military secret. It was issued by General -- Army General Veljko Kadijevic, who was the federal secretary of national defence, and it is entitled: "On the Use of the Armed Forces for the Preparation and Performance of Combat Activities in the Forthcoming Period." It leaves absolutely no doubt as to which ethnic group the JNA favoured. You will see, Your Honours, an excerpt from the text of that document. It says: "Our armed forces are entering a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war: The protection of the Serbian population ..." and it goes on. The second document, Your Honour, was issued four months later, approximately four months later, on the 20th of March, 1992, and it is entitled: "The Conclusions of the Evaluation of the Situation on the BiH Territory in the Zone of Responsibility of the 2nd Military District." This document, Your Honour, is a military secret. This document was sent directly to the attention of the chief of the JNA General Staff. It reflects -- if you can turn to the next portion, it reflects, Your Honours, that the directive of General Kadijevic was swiftly implemented in Bosnia, and you will see before Your Honours an excerpt from that document issued by General Kukanjac, who was the head of the 2nd Military District, a JNA general. And if you turn to the caption, this is: "Volunteer Units in the Zone of the 2nd Military District." Subpart B says there are 69.198 volunteers. And in subpart C, you'll see that the volunteer that he is referring to are not part of the formation, construction of the JNA or Territorial Defence. These are people who were outside of the army. If you go to subpart V, the JNA distributed 51.900 pieces of armament; 75 per cent in the SDS, which was the political party of Radovan Karadzic distributed 17.298 pieces. That's a total of 69.198 pieces of arms. G, subpart G reflects that 300 automatic rifles had been distributed in Sarajevo and others were going to be distributed in Sarajevo. Now, there was a key attached to General Kukanjac's report that described geographically where these volunteers were located; and you will see, Your Honour, it doesn't come up on one page, unfortunately, but in this attachment there are 75 municipalities in Bosnia or areas within municipalities where these arms were distributed. And appearing on the screen before you, you will see those areas where the arms and where the volunteers were. And if we go to the end of that particular document, you will see that this is 69.198. That's the number of arms that were distributed, and what's interesting to note about this document, Your Honours, is that one can see that arms were distributed by the JNA to Serb volunteers on a systematic and a widespread basis. It covered a large area of Bosnia, areas that -- many of which became part of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me now fast-forward to Bosnia six weeks after the report that was issued by General Kukanjac showing the distribution of arms in the 75 areas in Bosnia. On the 12th of May, six weeks after the Kukanjac report was issued, the Bosnian Serbs held the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb assembly. It was an important assembly session. It was important because it was at that session Radovan Karadzic announced the establishment of the VRS and announced that Radovan -- that Ratko Mladic would be serving as its head, and the announcement was made by Radovan Karadzic of the six strategic objectives of the Bosnian Serb people. Now, the six strategic objectives which are before Your Honours on the screen were the core political and military goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership. General Mladic, who attended the 16th Session, addressed the members of the assembly, and he said that he, too, had been involved in the formulation of these objectives, both with the "top leadership" of the Republika Srpska and "an even more select political leadership in Belgrade." Now, for purposes of this trial, Your Honours, the strategic objectives that are the most important are strategic objectives 1, 3, and 5. Strategic objective 1 was to -- an objective to separate the Serb communities from the non-Serbs in Bosnia. Strategic objective number 3 - if we could have the map in front of Your Honours - strategic objective number 3, Your Honours, is the establishment of a corridor in the Drina River Valley, that is, eliminate the Drina River as a border that separates Bosnia from Serbia. And strategic objective number 5 was to divide the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts and to establish effective state authorities in both parts. Now, Your Honours, the announcement of these strategic objectives was not an epiphany because a month and a half before their announcement, violent attacks had taken place against the Muslim community in the city of Bijeljina. Bijeljina, Your Honours, for your information, relates to strategic objective number 3. If you see the word "Semberija" on the right-hand side, slightly above the letter A, you'll locate the city of Bijeljina. What happened in Bijeljina was that paramilitary formations led by the notorious paramilitary leader Arkan attacked the Muslims in that community, took control of the municipality, and the JNA stood idly by and did not intervene. You'll receive evidence, as well, during the course of this trial that the JNA took an active role in ethnic cleansing, in cleansing non-Serbs from the territory that was coveted by the Bosnian Serbs. For example, on the 9th of May, in the Bratunac municipality -- and Bratunac, for your information, can be located next to the number 3 that says "Drina SO3." It sits along the border between Bosnia and Serbia. The JNA participated in the ethnic cleansing of the Muslim village of Glogova and the Muslim settlements in and around Bratunac. Elsewhere in Bosnia - this is before the strategic objectives were formally announced at the assembly - the pattern was the same. In the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, which is located in Western Bosnia - it's located above the word "Una" on the left-hand side of the map - the Bosnian Muslims were ethnically cleansed from the territory with the assistance of the JNA. At the 16th assembly session when the strategic objectives were announced, the assembly deputy from Bosanska Krupa, Miroslav Vjestica, reported to the fellow members of the assembly that "on the right bank of the Una river, there are no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa." The Prosecution evidence, Your Honour, will establish that the JNA played a critical role in that ethnic cleansing operation. Those are just some examples, Your Honour. We will present additional evidence relating to this topic. Now, these large-scale crimes, these ethnic cleansings that had happened along the eastern part of Bosnia and in other parts of Bosnia did not go unnoticed by the international community. Pressure was brought to bear on Belgrade authorities to withdraw the army from Bosnia, and on the 19th of May, 1992, the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in compliance with UN Resolution 752, withdrew their personnel, JNA personnel, from Bosnia and their equipment from Bosnia. Shortly thereafter, the JNA was renamed the Yugoslav Army, or the VJ. However, the withdrawal of the JNA was a sham. It did not end the agony in Bosnia as key Serb gains had to be solidified and other objectives had been obtained. In order to implement the state policy of the rump Yugoslavia of "creating conditions for the establishment of a single state of the Serbian people," the JNA left behind immense military reserves of equipment for use by the VRS; and thereafter, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the VJ provided the Bosnian Serbs and the Krajina Serbs with covert military assistance in violation of Yugoslav domestic law, in breach of UN resolutions, and contrary to public pronouncements by FRY political and military leaders. I intend to discuss this in greater detail later in my remarks. Now, I have presented this brief overview, Your Honour, so we could put into context the case against General Perisic when he, Your Honours, became the Chief of the General Staff and when he faithfully and without reservation implemented the policies of the FRY. Now, let me address, Your Honours, General Perisic's criminal responsibility under article 7.1 of the Statute. His criminal liability under 7.1 is based on his aiding and abetting the crimes charged in respect of Sarajevo and Srebrenica. Within the policies of the SDC and within the limitations set by the SDC, he provided extensive military aid to the VRS, which had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. The evidence will show that General Perisic was aware of the substantial likelihood that the military assistance provided to the VRS would assist in the commission of crimes. He aided and abetted these crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica in four ways: By supplying large quantities of weapons, ammunition, and other logistical materials without which the Bosnian Serb army could not have prosecuted the war; he deployed and supported -- and supported senior officers in the VRS; he sent regular VJ troops stationed in the FRY into Bosnia; and he aided and abetted the commission of crimes by consistently failing to fulfil his duty to prevent, investigate, and punish breaches of international law perpetrated by his subordinates serving in the Bosnian Serb army and the Serbian -- the Croatian Serb army, of which he was fully aware. And through this omission, this series of omissions, he created an environment of impunity wherein his subordinates were encouraged and did persist in committing crimes, knowing that there would be no consequences for their derelictions. Now, as I've stated earlier, Your Honours, the policy of Slobodan Milosevic's Yugoslavia was to support the war efforts of their Serb brethren in both Bosnia and in Croatia. They did so by providing massive quantities of military aid to the VRS and the SVK, including artillery weapons, small arms ammunition, small arms, communications equipment, and the like. This assistance was a carefully guarded state secret, since it was in breach of UN resolutions prohibiting the FRY from interfering in the affairs of Bosnia. The vital military assistance that was provided to the two armies in Bosnia and in Croatia occurred in two phases. The initial phase was that large volumes of material were left for the Bosnian Serb forces when the JNA officially left Bosnia in May of 1992. Thereafter, and until the end of the war, the VJ supplied the VRS with their essential military needs. This phase included the phase when General Perisic was Chief of the VJ General Staff. Now, what quantities am I talking about? Focusing solely on the infantry ammunition left behind by the VJ -- by the JNA, General Mladic at the 50th Session of the Bosnian Serb assembly, which was held on the 15th and 16th of April, 1995, estimated that 42.2 per cent of the total infantry ammunition consumed since the beginning of the war, which was 9.185 tonnes, had been inherited or found -- inherited from the JNA or found in the barracks. Now, in addition to that 42.2-per cent infantry ammunition, General Mladic specified the volume of material assistance the VJ had provided to the VRS. So in addition to the 42 per cent, he said that 47.2 per cent of the total infantry ammunition consumed from the beginning of the war was aid from -- received from the Yugoslav Army; 34.4 per cent of the 18.151 tonnes of artillery ammunition used by the VRS was from VJ aid. As the Chief of the VJ General Staff, General Perisic ordered a substantial amount of that military support be furnished to the VRS. Now, once again, Your Honour, I need to go into closed session. I'll do so briefly, but I need to refer to two exhibits.

Now, the Prosecution evidence will link munitions provided to the VRS to crimes alleged in the indictment. Expended ammunition, shell cartridges that were recovered by the Office of the Prosecutor at various execution sites identified in the schedule relating to Srebrenica, the massacre sites, were produced in the FRY at the that General Perisic was Chief of the VJ General Staff. Likewise, artillery fragments recovered at the sites of some of the scheduled shelling incidents and other incidents were produced in the FRY at the same time. Now, the fearsome war engine of the Bosnian Serbs would have collapsed without the assistance, the massive military assistance provided from the VJ and from the FRY. Again, I need to go into closed session very, very briefly. If I could have the Court's permission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours will receive evidence that, according to the accused, the volume of military assistance the VJ provided to the Bosnian Serb army and the Bosnian Croat army was so great that it imperilled the combat-readiness of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, let me turn to another element of -- where General Perisic aided and abetted. The indictment alleges that General Perisic continued the practice of providing, deploying, and supporting senior officers to the VRS. In order to achieve by military means the objectives that were sought by the leaders of the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, new armies had to be created, and they were created. The VRS was established on the 12th of May, 1992, and the SVK, Bosnian Croat Army, was established on the 16th of October, 1992. Their ranks filled with volunteers, many of whom had served in the Territorial Defence or who had served in the JNA. But these nascent armies were not capable of survival without substantial manpower and financial assistance from the FRY; and in order to sustain them, the JNA, and later the VJ, ordered its personnel to serve in those armies. In many cases, Your Honours, the VRS and the SVK requested the services of specifically identified officers, and they were given; or they requested officers who could fill specific needs of the army, and they were given. When General Perisic became Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, he continued the FRY policy of providing officers to serve in those armies, in deploying them to those armies, and in supporting them. He proposed - and I'll discuss this later - he proposed two temporary personnel formations be created: the 30th Personnel Centre and the 40th Personnel Centre. The 30th Personnel Centre was for persons serving in the Republika Srpska, and the 40th Personnel Centre was for VJ personnel serving in the SVK. The structure and the purpose of these personnel centres was an elaborate deception. It was a deception to disguise the provision and payment of these officers to those armies. If we turn to the next document, Your Honour, the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, you'll see on the organigramme in front of you was part of the VJ General Staff. The 30th and 40th Personnel Centres are the two boxes that appear at the bottom of the organigramme. They are part of the personnel administration, and they are part of the recruitment and mobilisation organ of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we zoom in? We can't read what is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution evidence will show that the VRS and the SVK command structures were made up of members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres. In its pre-trial brief, the Defence asserts that "The members of the VRS Main Staff and the VRS core commanders were not members of the VJ." That's found at the Defence pre-trial brief, page 44, subpart J. This is significant, and let me explain why. If we can -- the first document, the document that is before you, Your Honours, is the 30th Personnel Centre; and although the font is quite small, we can zoom in on it if you would like. It identifies VJ personnel who served in the 30th Personnel Centre and who made up the Bosnian Serb army command structure. So if we go -- if I can focus your attention, Your Honours, down to the first parallel group, these are the various organs of the VRS. These are the Department for Security and Intelligence Affairs, for example, the various staff organs of the VRS. And if we go down one lower, then Your Honours will see that the VJ personnel also made up a substantial part of the corps of the VRS, including the Drina Corps, whose area of responsibility was where the Srebrenica massacres took place, and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, whose commanders were General Milosevic and General Galic. Now, without members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres of the VJ making up part of the command structure, let me show you what the VRS command structure would look like. So in front of you is an organigramme showing you what the VRS command structure looked like without VJ officers from the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres. If we turn, Your Honours, to the next organigramme, which shows the 40th Personnel Centre officers or VJ officers within the SVK command structure, Your Honours will see this organigramme is set up in a similar way to the previous one, the first going from the bottom up. The long column going from left to right are the corps of the SVK. Above that are the organs of the SVK, and above that is the Superior Command of the SVK. I can blow that up if Your Honours wish. These are the corps, Your Honour. These are the VJ personnel from the 40th Personnel Centre who were in the SVK command structure. Your Honour, if we go up a level, these officers -- these are officers in the various organs of the SVK, and if we go up to the two levels -- the two levels above that, Your Honours will see this is the higher echelon of the SVK. The command at the top is the commanders of the Main Staff of the SVK, and the box to the lower -- to the left are the assistant commanders and the Chief of the General Staff of the SVK. Now, Your Honours, what would that command structure look like without VJ officers from the 40th Personnel Centre? The next organigramme shows Your Honours what that command structure would look like without VJ officers from the 40th Personnel Centre. We also allege, Your Honour, in the indictment that General Perisic aided and abetted the crimes in the indictment by, in some instances, ordering regular VJ troops stationed in the FRY into Bosnia. We will lead evidence, Your Honour, about one such operation. "Pancir-2" was the name of the operation. It occurred in late 1993 and early 1994. And the purpose of Pancir-2 was to take the high ground, Mount Zuc that overlooked Sarajevo. It was important for the VRS in their efforts to achieve military control over Sarajevo. We'll take a look, Your Honour, at the first exhibit before you. This is as -- or the first piece before you, Your Honour. We have identified the location of Mount Zuc, and Your Honours can see in the much -- toward the bottom the much denser area below the dark is the city of Sarajevo. So Mount Zuc, if we can go to the next document, you'll have a better view of Mount Zuc. You'll see in this aerial image the city of Sarajevo, which runs diagonally, and there's a large mountain formation to the left of the city overlooking the city. That's Mount Zuc. And in order to achieve, in order to take that mountain, General Perisic ordered members of the VJ special forces to the Sarajevo front. The VJ special core units, including the Guards Brigade, the 72nd Special Corps Units, the 72nd Brigade, and the 63rd Parachute Brigade, were directly subordinated to the VJ of the General Staff, to General Perisic, and he had authority to order their engagement and use in combat. Now, the Office of the Prosecutor asked General Perisic about the participation of VJ troops in Bosnia and in Sarajevo. In written responses to questions put to him about that subject, in his recorded suspect interview, and in his pre-trial brief, General Perisic denied that the VJ was involved in operations in Bosnia during the time he was Chief of the VJ General Staff or that he ever ordered VJ units into operation in Bosnia. He stated that "volunteer or renegade troops" may have left the FRY and operated in and around Sarajevo, but they did not commit any crimes alleged in the indictment. General Perisic was untruthful in his responses. If we can turn to the next document, Your Honour, the next document -- if we turn to the next document, Your Honour, this is a document from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps command, and it is an order to carry out an operation. It's dated the 3rd of November, 1993, and it's to all the commanders, and you'll see in subpart 1 the units that will be taking place -- taking part in that operation. You'll see it says at the end of the -- the bottom of that page, it says: "VJ Special Forces up to 120 people and a helicopter squad." And if we go further down in that order, you'll see that the operation was to be carried out in two stages. The first stage was the capture of Zuc. Now, Your Honours, the presence of VJ troops operating in Bosnia approximately seven months after the JNA had officially withdrawn from Bosnia was a flagrant violation of undertakings made by Slobodan Milosevic, one that could have exposed the FRY to grave - graver, I should say - consequences. For that reason, the FRY and the VRS took considerable efforts to hide the participation of VJ units in Bosnia. This is reflected in the next document I'm going to present. This next document, Your Honour, it is -- you'll see from the -- I'm going to show you different parts of this document. The first part of this document, Your Honour, this is from the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska. It was issued by the Deputy Commander of the VRS, General Milovanovic, and it is very urgent. If we go to the next part of this document, you'll see what it was that was very urgent. It is a warning, and the warning says, and I go to the second sentence: "In order to protect confidentiality and other measures and activities that we have been undertaking, I forbid the use of or any reference in regular and telephone communications to the term Yugoslav Army units." It goes on to the next page to say at the top: "The Yugoslav Army units shall be treated as reserve forces of the General Staff, the VRS Main Staff, regardless of their size, type, or strength." In other words, don't refer to the VJ troops; refer to them as VRS reserve units. Now, normal circumstances, I suspect, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commanders would have respected that warning. But if we turn to the next document, you'll see that they did not. When members of the VJ Special unit, the 72nd Special Brigade, participated in the attack on Mount Zuc, Your Honours, they suffered considerable casualties, and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps commander, General Galic, reported that. This is a report from General Galic. It's dated the 27th of December, 1993, and it says: "On the 27th of December, in accordance with Operation Pancir-2, a planned attack by combat groups under the command of Colonel Stupar, commander of the 72nd Brigade of the VJ," the Yugoslav Army, "was carried out." Now, if we go down to the next part of this document, General Galic then reports that they sustained casualties, and you'll see in this section that I'm illustrating on your monitors that seven members of the 72nd Brigade were killed, and the rest of them managed to pull out with difficulties. It also goes on to say that ten of them were wounded. Now, these casualties -- VJ casualties were recorded in VJ military documents, and they were recorded in obituaries that were in -- that appeared in newspapers in Belgrade. One example, Your Honour, I'll show you of this is an obituary for a captain of the Yugoslav Army whose obituary you have before you on the monitor. According to one of the obituaries, it says that this young man, who was a captain in the Yugoslav Army, "who died a heroic death on 27 December 1993, defending his country, the Greater Serbia." Our evidence will show, Your Honour, that on the 27th of December, 1993, when the VJ special units were assaulting Mount Zuc - and you've seen their proximity to Sarajevo -- Mount Zuc's proximity to Sarajevo - that the VRS conducted an artillery barrage on the city centre itself of great intensity. Approximately 600 shells fell on the centre of Sarajevo, and at least 7 persons were killed and 58 others were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have previously addressed the fourth manner in which General Perisic aided and abetted in the commission of the crimes, that is, by consistently failing in his duty to prevent, to investigate, and to punish breaches of international law committed by his subordinates serving in the VRS and the SVK, and I won't go further on that topic. Instead, I'd like to turn to General Perisic's responsibility under Article 7.3 of the Statute of the Tribunal. General Perisic is charged in all counts with 7.3, criminal responsibility. Now, quite obviously his responsibility to prevent the criminal conduct of his subordinates extended until the war ended, which was the signing of the Dayton Agreements. His criminal liability to punish, however, extended for a considerable period longer. It extended throughout the period he was Chief of the VJ General Staff, that is, through November the 24th, 1998. In order to establish his criminal responsibility under Article 7.3, the Prosecution has to establish three elements: That a superior-subordinate relationship existed between General Perisic and his subordinates who committed the crimes; that General Perisic knew or had reason to know that a criminal act was about to be or had been committed; and that he failed to take reasonable and necessary measures to prevent the criminal act from occurring or to punish the perpetrators who committed them. Now, one of the principal issues that will be before Your Honours in this case is whether a superior-subordinate relationship existed between General Perisic and the officers who were members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, the special formations that I've identified that were part of the VJ General Staff structure. Our position is that they were; the Defence position is that they were not his subordinates. Now, his subordinates, as you have seen from the organigrammes that I have presented, included General Mladic, General Krstic, General Milosevic, General Galic, and others. In order, Your Honour, to prove a superior-subordinate relationship, it's incumbent on the Prosecution to establish that General Perisic had effective control, meaning that he had the ability -- the material ability to prevent or punish the commission of the offences. Now, when assessing the various elements in the evidentiary matrix that make up effective control, I want to draw Your Honours' attention to one point, and that is that General Perisic did not exercise operational control over his subordinates in the SVK and VRS -- the VRS and the SVK. And by "operational control," what I mean is exercising command and control through issuing orders, commands, instructions, directives for military combat operations being conducted in the field. In fact, operational control had de facto been delegated to the commanders of the VRS and the SVK, and this created a situation where they, as well as Perisic, had the material ability to prevent and punish the criminal conduct of seconded VJ officers. In other words, General Perisic's material ability to prevent and punish criminal conduct of VJ officers was parallel and concurrent to the material ability held by the commanders of the VRS and the SVK who had operational control of these officers and who also had a superior-subordinate relationship with them. For example, Radovan Karadzic was the Supreme Commander of the VRS. He had the material ability to punish his subordinates in the VRS, including soldiers seconded to that army from the VJ. If General Perisic was aware that his subordinates had committed crimes while serving in the VRS and he was aware that President Karadzic failed to sanction those offenders, General Perisic's responsibility to do so was not extinguished because of Karadzic's indifference or his inaction. General Perisic was obliged to take action against his VJ subordinates. Now, you've heard a lot about the 30th and the 40th Personnel Centres. Let me turn to the creation and the purpose of those centres. This has a direct bearing on both General Perisic's criminal responsibility under Article 7.1 and also 7.3. Before General Perisic became Chief of the VJ General Staff, members of the JNA and members of the VJ had volunteered to serve in the two armies in Bosnia and Croatia, or they were transferred from the VJ and the JNA to serve in those armies. The salaries of those officers were paid to them by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia throughout the period of the war with one exception, and that is following the Republika Srpska's failure to accept the Contact Group Peace Plan in 1994. There was a brief interruption in the payment of salaries. The law on the VJ permitted an officer in the VJ to serve outside the borders of the FRY in two circumstances: as part of an international peace-keeping force or in diplomatic postings. General Perisic was aware that neither one of those conditions applied to VJ personnel who were serving in the VRS or the SVK or would apply to soldiers he was going to deploy there in the future. In his suspect interview, General Perisic said, and he acknowledged that those -- and I'm quoting, those who would be dispatching VJ soldiers to participate in the war in Bosnia "would be breaking a law." To rectify this problem, General Perisic proposed that special personnel centres be created. One of the important issues that Your Honours will deal with in this case was what was the nature of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres? In his suspect interview, General Perisic described the personnel centres. He said it was merely "one office" that was based in the personnel administration of the General Staff and was staffed with "2 or 3" men. According to General Perisic - and I'm putting up on the screen, Your Honour, an excerpt from his written responses to questions that were put to him - according to General Perisic, these -- and I'm quoting, "These centres were formed in late 1993 by order of the VSO" -- that's Supreme Defence Council -- "for the purpose of drawing up complete records indicating which individuals, former JNA/VJ members born in Croatia and Bosnia joined the Army of Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina as volunteers." And also: "... all other JNA/VJ members that joined these armies on a volunteer basis. Precise records were needed for the following reasons..." and he then lists the reasons. In his suspect interview, General Perisic went on to define the term "volunteer." He defined it this way: "People who voluntarily, without any influence of anyone but out of their will, want to go and perform a certain job and task." Now, Prosecution evidence will show that the nature of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres was considerably different. The 30th and 40th Personnel Centres were created as legal cover to hide the fact that the VJ was ordering its personnel to serve in Bosnia and in Croatia in contravention of FRY law and in contravention of international undertakings and obligations. If we can go into closed session, please.
